metaDesc: A real 2-day cross-province plan for Suphan Buri and Ang Thong, Thailand: pay respects at Wat Pa Lelai, the giant Buddha at Wat Muang, and the reclining Buddha at Wat Khun Inthapramun, plus old riverside markets. Real routes, real timing.

h1:
Suphan Buri–Ang Thong
2 Days of Temples & Rivers
intro: These two provinces sit only about 44 kilometres apart, an easy drive between them, so it makes sense to roll them into one trip. Day one covers Suphan Buri: pay your respects to the great Buddha at Wat Pa Lelai and wander the century-old Sam Chuk market. Day two crosses into Ang Thong for the giant Buddha at Wat Muang and the reclining Buddha at Wat Khun Inthapramun, then winds down at San Chao Rong Thong market on the banks of the Noi River. This plan is built from a route you can actually drive, with no rushing.

blocks.html: Suphan Buri and Ang Thong pair up better than you might expect. Both sit on the flat central river plain, both have old temples, oversized Buddha images, and riverside markets that are still very much alive. Driving from downtown Suphan Buri to downtown Ang Thong takes only about an hour, which makes it ideal for an unhurried temple trip: spend one night in Suphan Buri, then take on Ang Thong the next morning. We've laid it out across two days, full enough to be worth it but never exhausting.

This trip suits anyone driving their own car, because the temples in Ang Thong are spread across different districts and public transport between them is awkward. If you don't have your own wheels, renting a car or hiring a van by the day will be far smoother.

items: Day 1 — Suphan Buri: Wat Pa Lelai → Banharn-Jaemsai Tower → Sam Chuk Century-Old Market → overnight in Suphan Buri town
Day 2 — Ang Thong: Wat Muang (giant Buddha) → Wat Khun Inthapramun (reclining Buddha) → San Chao Rong Thong market → head home
Total distance: Suphan Buri to Ang Thong is about 44 km; the stops within each day are mostly 10–20 km apart, so it's all short drives
Good for: temple lovers, families travelling with older relatives, and anyone who enjoys old markets and local food

blocks.title: Before you set off
blocks.html: Most temples open from morning to evening (roughly 8am–5pm), but the midday sun is brutal, especially at Wat Muang and Wat Khun Inthapramun where the big Buddha images sit out in the open. Aim for the morning or late afternoon for better photos and gentler heat.

blocks.title: Book the activities in your Suphan Buri trip ahead
blocks.text: Booking online ahead on Klook or GetYourGuide is usually cheaper than the gate and skips the queue. Pick only the experiences you actually want — prices and availability are shown live on each site.

blocks.text: Day 1 — Suphan Buri: the great Buddha and a century-old market

items.activity: Leave Bangkok, head for downtown Suphan Buri
items.note: From Bangkok it's about 100–120 km, roughly 1.5–2 hours depending on where you start. Grab breakfast on the way or eat once you're in town.

items.activity: Wat Pa Lelai Worawihan — pay respects to the great Buddha
items.note: A large Buddha image in the Pa Lelai pose, about 23 metres tall, in a temple tied to the classic Thai epic Khun Chang Khun Phaen. Khum Khun Phaen, a recreated traditional house, is right next door to explore.

items.activity: Lunch — fish or duck noodles in town
items.note: Suphan Buri is known for fish noodles and boat noodles, and they're easy to find around town. Expect roughly THB 40–80 a bowl.

items.activity: Banharn-Jaemsai Tower for a view over the city
items.note: A tower in Chaloem Phatara Rachini Park; head up for a 360-degree view over Suphan Buri. Entry is just a few tens of baht, perfect for a quick stop.

An old market on the banks of the Tha Chin River, with its wooden shophouse rows still intact. There are snacks, old-school coffee, and Thai sweets, easy to wander all afternoon. It's busiest on weekends.

items.activity: Check in to your hotel in Suphan Buri town and rest
items.note: Downtown has hotels and stays at a range of prices. Picking one near a main road makes finding dinner easy.

blocks.html: Day one is meant to stay light, without racing between temples, because day two in Ang Thong has more big Buddha images and walking to do. If you reach Suphan Buri early and still have energy, you could add Bueng Chawak Chaloem Phrakiat (out in Doembang Nangbuat district), but it sits in the opposite direction from the road to Ang Thong, so we left it out of the main plan.

blocks.text: Day 2 — Crossing into Ang Thong: giant Buddha, reclining Buddha, riverside market

items.activity: Breakfast, check out, and leave Suphan Buri
items.note: The Suphan Buri–Ang Thong route is about 44 km, roughly 1 hour, and an easy drive.

items.activity: Wat Muang — pay respects to the giant Buddha
items.note: In Wiset Chai Chan district, about 8 km from Ang Thong town. The seated Buddha, Phra Phuttha Maha Nawamin, has a lap width of around 62 metres and is one of the largest in Thailand. The temple grounds also have model heaven-and-hell scenes to walk through. Go in the morning before it gets too hot.

items.activity: Stop at San Chao Rong Thong market for lunch
items.note: An old market on the banks of the Noi River in Wiset Chai Chan district, close to Wat Muang. It has local food, khanom chin (rice noodles), noodles, and souvenirs, an easy spot for an unhurried lunch.

items.activity: Wat Khun Inthapramun — the open-air reclining Buddha
items.note: In Pho Thong district. The reclining Buddha (Phra Phuttha Saiyat), out in the open, is about 50 metres long, one of the longest in the country. It's an old temple tied to local legend.

items.activity: Stop at Wat Ton Son or riverside Wat Tha Sutthawat (if there's time)
items.note: Ang Thong town has riverside temples to visit if you want to keep going. If you're worn out, skip them; nothing here is mandatory.

items.activity: Pick up souvenirs and head home
items.note: From Ang Thong back to Bangkok is about 100 km, roughly 2 hours, or you can carry on to nearby Ayutthaya instead.

blocks.title: On what to wear
blocks.html: Every temple in this plan is a sacred site, so dress respectfully: no spaghetti straps and no very short shorts, especially if you plan to go in and pay respects inside the ordination hall. Keeping a shawl or wrap in the car is a smart move.

blocks.text: Food you shouldn't miss in both provinces

items.name: Suphan Buri fish noodles & boat noodles
items.blurb: The signature dish of Suphan Buri: a rich broth, fresh fish, served clear or as 'nam tok' (with blood added). You'll find it all over town, ideal for breakfast or lunch on day one.

items.name: Sweets at Sam Chuk market
items.blurb: The century-old market has Thai sweets, old-school coffee, Mae La snakehead fish, and retro snacks. Easy to graze on all afternoon.

items.name: Eats at San Chao Rong Thong market
items.blurb: An old market on the Noi River on the Ang Thong side, with khanom chin, noodles, khanom chin with wild-herb curry, and old Thai-Chinese sweets. Great for lunch on day two.

items.name: Mae La snakehead fish
items.blurb: Firm-fleshed snakehead from the wetlands around Ang Thong and Sing Buri, done grilled, in tom yum, or in curry. It's a local staple that restaurants around here do well.

items.name: Chinese sausage & mooncake souvenirs
items.blurb: Both provinces have local Thai-Chinese souvenirs you can take home, sold at the old markets and souvenir shops in town.

blocks.html: This plan suggests spending the first night in downtown Suphan Buri, since it's the bigger town with hotels and stays at a range of prices and easy access to dinner. Then you drive into Ang Thong the next morning, which takes only about an hour. If you'd rather spend longer in Ang Thong, you could just as easily flip it and stay on the Ang Thong side for the second night before heading home.

items.name: Stays in Suphan Buri town
items.blurb: Pick somewhere near a main road or near Wat Pa Lelai so the next day's drive is easy. Options run from budget hotels to mid-range.

items.name: Stays in Ang Thong town
items.blurb: An option if you want to keep temple-hopping in Ang Thong over several days. The town is small but has riverside stays to choose from.

blocks.text: Tips to make the trip smoother

items: Avoid the midday heat — the big Buddha images in Ang Thong are out in the open, so going in the morning or late afternoon is more comfortable and makes for better photos.
Carry cash — shops in the old markets and many temples take cash or PromptPay; not everywhere accepts cards.
Allow time for driving — the temples in Ang Thong are in different districts, 10–20 km apart. Use a navigation app and build in some buffer.
You can extend the trip — Ang Thong is close to Ayutthaya, so if you're not ready to head home, drive on and spend another day in Ayutthaya.

faq.q: How far apart are Suphan Buri and Ang Thong, and is it a long drive?
faq.a: From downtown Suphan Buri to downtown Ang Thong is about 44 kilometres, roughly a 1-hour drive on an easy route, so it's no trouble to combine the two provinces into a single trip.

faq.q: Do I need my own car for this trip?
faq.a: We'd recommend driving yourself or hiring a car, because the temples in Ang Thong are in different districts, 10–20 kilometres apart, and public transport between them is awkward. If you don't have a car, renting one or hiring a van by the day will be much smoother.

faq.q: Which temples in Ang Thong shouldn't I miss?
faq.a: The three main ones are Wat Muang (a giant seated Buddha with a lap width of around 62 metres), Wat Khun Inthapramun (an open-air reclining Buddha about 50 metres long), and San Chao Rong Thong market on the Noi River for local food.

faq.q: Which province should I stay in?
faq.a: This plan suggests staying in downtown Suphan Buri the first night, since it's the bigger town with stays and restaurants at a range of prices, then driving into Ang Thong the next morning, which takes only about an hour.

faq.q: When is the best time to take this trip?
faq.a: You can go year-round, but the cool season (November–February) is the most comfortable and best for walking around the open-air temples. Sam Chuk and San Chao Rong Thong markets are busiest on weekends.
